answer_text:
The expression is defined for probabilities in \((0,1)\), so the limit is understood as \(x\to0^+\).

Let
\[
\bar\Phi(t)=1-\Phi(t),\qquad \phi(t)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-t^2/2}.
\]

We use the standard Mills ratio asymptotic for the standard normal tail:
\[
\bar\Phi(t)\sim \frac{\phi(t)}{t}
=\frac{e^{-t^2/2}}{t\sqrt{2\pi}},\qquad t\to\infty.
\]

Now let \(p\downarrow0\) and set
\[
t_p=\Phi^{-1}(1-p),
\]
so that \(\bar\Phi(t_p)=p\). Using the Mills ratio,
\[
p=\bar\Phi(t_p)\sim \frac{e^{-t_p^2/2}}{t_p\sqrt{2\pi}}.
\]
Taking logs gives
\[
\ln\frac1p
= \frac{t_p^2}{2}+\ln t_p+\frac12\ln(2\pi)+o(1).
\]
Since \(\ln t_p=o(t_p^2)\), this implies
\[
t_p=\sqrt{2\ln\frac1p}\,(1+o(1)).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\Phi^{-1}(1-p)=\sqrt{2\ln\frac1p}\,(1+o(1)),\qquad p\downarrow0.
\]

Apply this first to \(p=x\):
\[
\Phi^{-1}(1-x)
=
\sqrt{2\ln\frac1x}\,(1+o(1)).
\]

Next apply it to \(p=x/n\):
\[
\Phi^{-1}\!\left(1-\frac{x}{n}\right)
=
\sqrt{2\ln\frac{n}{x}}\,(1+o(1))
=
\sqrt{2\left(\ln\frac1x+\ln n\right)}\,(1+o(1)).
\]

Therefore,
\[
\frac{\Phi^{-1}(1-x)}{\Phi^{-1}(1-x/n)}
=
\frac{\sqrt{2\ln(1/x)}(1+o(1))}
{\sqrt{2(\ln(1/x)+\ln n)}(1+o(1))}.
\]
Since \(\ln n\) is fixed and \(\ln(1/x)\to\infty\),
\[
\frac{\ln(1/x)}{\ln(1/x)+\ln n}\to1.
\]
Hence the limit is
\[
\boxed{1}.
\]
